passages.title: Winds and angels swear the promise is certain
passages.tafsir:
Surah al-Mursalat opens with a chain of five oaths. Allah swears by five things that the Qur'an never names — it gives only their attributes, one after another — and then, in ayah 7, delivers the single sentence the whole chain was built to carry: *"Surely, what you are promised will come to pass."* Everything before ayah 7 is the swearing; ayah 7 is, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the subject of these oaths." That is what binds these seven ayat into one unit: six lines of rising tension, and one line that lands.

## The cave at Mina

Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both open this surah with the same scene, and it is worth sitting with. Al-Bukhari recorded from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud that he said:

> "While we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a cave at Mina, *wal-Mursalat* was revealed to him. He was reciting it and I was learning it from his mouth. Verily, his mouth was moist with it when a snake leaped out at us. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'Kill it!' So we quickly went after it, but it got away. Then the Prophet ﷺ said, 'It was saved from your harm just as you all were saved from its harm.'"

Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim also recorded this hadith, by way of al-Aʿmash.

Notice what the scene contains. A surah about the certain arrival of the Last Day comes down not in a moment of grandeur but in a cave, in the middle of an ordinary fright — and Ibn Masʿud is standing close enough to catch the words off the Prophet's ﷺ lips while they are still moist with them. Revelation and daily life are not in separate rooms. And the Prophet's ﷺ closing remark about the snake is its own quiet lesson: he read the escape from both sides at once, ours and the creature's.

There is a second report Ibn Kathir places here. Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, from his mother, that she heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting *wal-Mursalat ʿurfa* in the Maghrib prayer. In the report from Malik, Umm al-Fadl heard her son Ibn ʿAbbas reciting this surah and said to him: "O my son! You reminded me with your recitation of this Surah. Verily, it is the last thing I heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He recited it in the Maghrib prayer." Ibn Kathir adds the note that this was before he ﷺ died, and states that both al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded the report in the Two Sahihs, by way of Malik.

So this surah is the last thing Umm al-Fadl heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — heard at Maghrib, near the end of his life. And her own son's recitation of it, later, brought that back to her.

## What, exactly, is Allah swearing by?

Here is the interesting difficulty. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, the Qur'an does not name the phenomena being sworn by. It gives only five *attributes*. Rendered plainly, in Maʿārif's own translation without any explanatory brackets:

1. by those that are sent one after the other (ayah 1)
2. and by those that blow violently (ayah 2)
3. and by those that spread all over (ayah 3)
4. and by those who differentiate distinctly (ayah 4)
5. then bring down the advice (ayah 5)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states frankly that there is no traceable hadith giving the exact interpretation of these phenomena. That absence is why the Companions and their pupils genuinely differed — and this is a difference of understanding, not of creed. The main positions:

**All five are angels.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Abu Hurayrah said of *al-Mursalat ʿurfa*: "The angels." Ibn Kathir reports similar statements from Masruq, Abu ad-Duha, Mujahid (in one narration from him), as-Suddi and ar-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. Abu Salih likewise took *al-ʿAsifat*, *an-Nashirat*, *al-Fariqat* and *al-Mulqiyat* all to mean the angels. Maʿārif adds that some held that different groups of angels are the bearers of the different attributes.

**All refer to the winds.** Ath-Thawri narrated from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, from Muslim al-Batin, from Abu al-ʿUbaydayn, that he asked Ibn Masʿud about *al-Mursalat ʿurfa* and Ibn Masʿud said: "The wind." He said the same of *al-ʿAsifat ʿasfa* and *an-Nashirat nashra*. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah are reported to have said the same.

**They are the Prophets and Messengers.** This is reported from Abu Salih in one narration, and Maʿārif notes that some authorities on tafsir held that the attributes refer to Allah's Prophets and Messengers.

**Other readings of single words.** Abu Salih is also reported as saying *an-Nashirat nashra* is the rain.

**Ibn Jarir at-Tabari's caution.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Jarir confidently affirmed that *al-ʿAsifat ʿasfa* means the wind, following Ibn Masʿud, but did not affirm whether *an-Nashirat nashra* are the angels or the wind. Maʿārif summarises his stance on the question as a whole: both possibilities exist, and he preferred not to side with any particular interpretation — in this matter, he said, it is safer to observe silence. That restraint is itself a scholarly lesson.

**Ibn Kathir's position — and why Maʿārif follows it.** Ibn Kathir divides the five: in the first three ayat Allah swears by various types of wind; in ayat 4 and 5 He swears by the angels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this approach "the best," and gives the reason plainly: some of the attributes are more appropriately applicable to the angels and cannot fit the winds without an unusual stretch of imagination, while others are more appropriately applicable to the winds and cannot apply to angels without a fanciful stretch. Read Ibn Kathir's way, Maʿārif says, the passage is "plain and simple, and does not require any undue stretch of imagination."

## Feeling the words

**al-Mursalat (ayah 1)** — every rendering in these two commentaries puts it in the passive: "those that are sent," "sent forth successively." Not the ones that blow, or move, or arrive: the ones *sent*. Ibn Kathir grounds the wind-reading in exactly that, citing *"And We send the winds fertilizing"* (15:22) and *"And it is He Who sends the winds as heralds of glad tidings, going before His mercy"* (7:57). In the ayat Ibn Kathir brings, wind is dispatched.

**ʿurfan** — Maʿārif gives two senses. It could signify "beneficial and useful," and the winds that bring rain are obviously that. Or it can mean "one after another," in which case ayah 1 means those winds that bring rain and clouds consecutively. The translation given here — "sent forth successively" — takes the second sense; Maʿārif presents both without ruling either out.

**ʿasifat, from ʿasf (ayah 2)** — Maʿārif: the word is derived from *ʿasf*, which literally means "winds that blow violently or vehemently," and it refers to the fiercely blowing winds that sometimes do occur in the world. Ibn Kathir adds a detail from Arabic usage: winds are called *ʿasifat* when they make noise with their blowing. So the word has a sound in it.

**nashirat (ayah 3)** — Maʿārif: the winds that spread the clouds all over after the rain is over. Ibn Kathir: the winds that scatter into clouds in the horizons of the sky — and he adds the crucial qualifier, *according to the will of the Lord*. Nothing up there is drifting.

**fariqat (ayah 4)** — the translation here is "those angels fully distinguishing truth from falsehood"; Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "the Fariqat that separate." He says the meaning is the angels, and on this he reports no difference of opinion, citing Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Masruq, Mujahid, Qatadah, ar-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, as-Suddi and ath-Thawri. What do they separate? Truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, the lawful from the forbidden.

**mulqiyat dhikran (ayah 5)** — "those delivering revelation," or in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "the Mulqiyat that remind." Maʿārif explains that *dhikr*, "Reminder," refers to the Qur'an, or to revelation in general.

Now look at how ayat 4 and 5 fit together, because this is the quiet heart of the passage. The angels do not separate truth from falsehood by some independent power of judgment. Ibn Kathir says they are the ones who descend with Allah's command to the Messengers, separating between truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, and the lawful and the forbidden. Maʿārif says the same thing in one breath, folding both ayat into a single sentence: "I swear by angels who [by bringing down revelation] separate between truth and falsehood, right and wrong, [and the lawful and the forbidden]." The separating and the delivering are one act. Revelation is the blade.

And Maʿārif's rendering of ayah 5 keeps the movement audible — not "and," but "*then* bring down the advice."

## Ayah 6: mercy at one end, warning at the other

*ʿUdhran aw nudhran* — "ending excuses and giving warnings," or as Maʿārif renders it, "to provide excuses [for the believers] or giving warnings [to disbelievers]." Maʿārif explains that this phrase is a complement to ayah 5: the "advice" of ayah 5 is the revelation that came down upon the Prophets, and ayah 6 tells us what that revelation is *for*. It serves two purposes, depending on who receives it. In the case of the people of truth and the believers, it persuades them to seek excuse from Allah for their shortcomings and to pray for forgiveness. In the case of the people of falsehood and the disbelievers, it contains a warning of Allah's torment if they oppose His command. Ibn Kathir says the same in his own words: the angels bring the revelation to the Messengers, which contains exemption or absolvement for the creatures and a warning for them of Allah's torment if they oppose His command.

One book, two effects. The *aw*, "or," is not vagueness — it is one revelation meeting two kinds of heart.

## Why winds first, then angels?

If ayat 1–3 are winds and ayat 4–5 are angels, a fair question arises: what connects them? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers with proper humility first — it is not possible to fathom the Wisdom of Divine speech — and then offers a hypothesis worth carrying with you.

Allah swears by useful winds and by harmful winds: the ones that bring rain and clouds, and the ones that blow fiercely and cause destruction. Both belong to the *perceptible* world; all human beings can observe them. The perceptible things are mentioned first, for reflection. The imperceptible world — the angels, revelation — is mentioned later. And Maʿārif draws the conclusion: if man reflects carefully on the first, he will develop certainty of belief in the second as well.

That is a whole method of faith folded into five lines. Begin with what lands on your face; arrive at what you cannot see.

## Ayah 7: what all of it was for

*Innama tuʿaduna la-waqiʿ* — "Surely, what you are promised will come to pass." Ibn Kathir marks this precisely: "This is the subject of these oaths." Everything before it was the run-up; this is the statement.

And he unpacks what "what you are promised" contains: the establishment of the Hour, the blowing of the horn, the resurrection of the bodies, the gathering of those of old and those of latter times on one common ground, and the rewarding of every doer of a deed based upon his deed — if he did good, then his reward will be good; if he did evil, then his reward will be evil. "All of this will occur," he says, "meaning it will come to pass and there is no avoiding it." Maʿārif states it just as flatly: the Day of Judgment, Reckoning, and Reward and Punishment that is promised by the Prophets (peace be upon them) has certainly to be fulfilled.

Promised by whom? Maʿārif's paraphrase answers it in passing — by the Prophets (peace be upon them). And on ayah 6 the same commentary says the "advice" of ayah 5 is "the revelation that came down upon the Prophets," while Ibn Kathir says of ayat 4–6 that the angels "bring the revelation to the Messengers." Three statements from the two commentaries, sitting next to each other. The promise sworn to in ayah 7 is not an anonymous one.

Ibn Kathir heads this whole section "Allah's swearing by Different Creatures about the Occurrence of the Hereafter" — the created world itself summoned to testify to a truth about the world to come.

From ayah 8 onward the surah stops asserting and starts showing: the stars losing their light, the heaven cleft asunder, the mountains blown away — all of it converging on the Day of Sorting Out. Our passage ends at the promise; what follows is the scene.

## Carrying it

**Let the weather do its work.** Maʿārif's reading makes ayat 1–3 an invitation, not decoration. The winds belong to the perceptible world; every human being can observe them, and they are the first witness Allah calls. The rain-bearing wind and the destroying wind are both *sent*. And Maʿārif's promise is exactly this: careful reflection on what you can perceive builds certainty in what you cannot.

**Take revelation as ʿudhr before it becomes nudhr.** Maʿārif's explanation is directly practical: what the Qur'an does in the life of a believer is persuade him to seek excuse from Allah for his shortcomings and to pray for forgiveness. If reading it produces that in you, it is doing in you what ayah 6 says it does.

**Weigh ayah 7 honestly.** Ibn Kathir's summary of the promise is even-handed: good deeds rewarded with good, evil with evil, and the people of old and of later times gathered on one common ground. The passage does not ask for panic. It asks you to stop treating the Day as a maybe.

**And it belongs in prayer.** The last thing Umm al-Fadl heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was this surah, recited in the Maghrib prayer. There is an invitation in that — for a surah said aloud, at the end of a day, in the hearing of one's family.

passages.title: Cosmic collapse and the Day of Decision
passages.tafsir:
**The sūrah opened with a series of oaths (ayat 1–6) and then said what they were sworn upon: "Surely, what you are promised will occur" (ayah 7). Ayat 8–15 are that promise unfolded — four world-ending events, a question about which Day they are being held for, and the answer: the Day of Decision.**

What binds these eight ayat into one unit is a single unfinished sentence. Ayat 8–11 pile up four clauses beginning with *when* — when the stars are put out, when the sky is torn open, when the mountains are blown away, when the Messengers' appointed time comes. Then, instead of completing the sentence, ayah 12 breaks in with a question: *for which Day has all this been set?* Ayah 13 answers in a single short phrase — for the Day of Decision. Ayah 14 refuses to let that answer settle into a familiar phrase. Ayah 15 pronounces the verdict on those who called it a lie.

## What exactly was promised

Ibn Kathir spells out what "what you are promised" in ayah 7 covers: the establishment of the Hour, the blowing of the horn, the resurrection of the bodies, the gathering of those of old and those of later times onto one common ground, and the rewarding of every doer of a deed based upon his deed — "if he did good, then his reward will be good, and if he did evil, then his reward will be evil." His summary is blunt: "All of this will occur, meaning it will come to pass and there is no avoiding it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other direction: the Day of Judgment, Reckoning, Reward and Punishment "that is promised by the Prophets" has certainly to be fulfilled. That is the claim. Ayat 8–11 are Allah's own description of what its arrival will look like — what Ibn Kathir heads as "a mention of some of what will occur on the Day of Judgement."

## Ayah 8 — the stars put out

Ibn Kathir glosses the verb simply: "their light will leave." He sets the ayah beside two sister verses — "And when the stars fall" (81:2) and "And when the stars have fallen and scattered" (82:2).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possible senses of the same statement: the stars "will be extinguished, which could mean that they will be completely destroyed, or they will exist, but their lights will be lost." Either way the outcome is the same, and Maʿārif states it starkly — "in this way the entire world will be plunged in absolute darkness."

Sit with that for a moment. Of everything a person looks at and assumes will still be there tomorrow, the stars come close to the top of the list. Ayah 8 puts them out first.

## Ayah 9 — the sky torn open

The ayah means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that the heaven "is cleft asunder, becomes split, its sides fall and its edges become weak." Notice the sequence in his gloss: first a split, then the sides giving way, then the edges losing their strength. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists this plainly as "the second event to occur… the splitting of the sky."

## Ayah 10 — the mountains blown away

*Nusifat*, Ibn Kathir says, means "they will be removed and no sight or trace of them will remain." Not toppled, not shattered where they stand — removed, so that nothing is left to mark where they were. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the third event as the mountains being "blown away as dust."

Ibn Kathir cites two verses here. The first is 20:105: "And they ask you concerning the mountains: Say, 'My Lord will blast them and scatter them as particles of dust.'" Where ayah 10 states only that the mountains are blown away, this verse names whose act it is — "My Lord will blast them."

The second is 18:47: "And the Day We shall cause the mountains to pass away, and you will see the earth as a leveled plain, and We shall gather them all together so as to leave not one of them behind."

That last verse is doing more than confirming the imagery. It joins two things in one breath: the earth is left a leveled plain, *and* every single person is gathered on it — "not one of them behind." The landscape being cleared and the assembly being convened belong to the same moment.

## Ayah 11: the word the early commentators weighed

Then comes the fourth *when*, and it is not a piece of scenery at all: **"and when the Messengers are given their appointed time."** After stars, sky and mountains, the attention turns to the Prophets. It is also the ayah on which the early commentators left the most differing explanations, because *uqqitat* carries several possible senses.

Ibn Kathir gathers the early views without declaring any one of them the only correct reading:

- **"Gathered."** Al-ʿAwfi narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Zayd read it the same way and pointed to "On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers together" (5:109).
- **"Postponed."** This is Mujahid's reading.
- **"Promised."** Ath-Thawri narrated this from Manṣūr, from Ibrahim. Ibn Kathir observes that Ibrahim seems to hold this to be similar to 39:69 — "And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord; and the Book will be produced; and the Prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward; and it will be judged between them with truth, and they will not be wronged."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the word back to its root: *uqqitat* is derived from **tawqīt**, which primarily means "appointment of time." It then cites Zamakhsharī (as cited in *Rūḥ*) that the word signifies "to arrive at an appointed time," and judges that in this context the second meaning appears to be more appropriate. On that reading, Maʿārif explains, the ayah means that the appointed time for the Prophets and Messengers to assemble with their communities will arrive, "so that all matters concerning them may be decided."

Whichever rendering is taken — *gathered*, *postponed*, *promised*, or *arrived at the appointed time* — the readings converge on an appointment: Messengers and communities present at a time already fixed, for their matters to be decided.

## Ayat 12–13: the question and its answer

Ayah 12 asks: **"for which Day has all this been set?"** Ibn Kathir's text renders the question "for what Day are these signs postponed?" — held back to a later, already-fixed time.

He reads the question as flowing directly out of ayah 11: "for which day are the Messengers postponed and their matter expected, so that the Hour will be established?" The broader rendering and this narrower one are both held in the wording, since the delay of the Messengers' matter and the delay of the cosmic upheaval are the same delay.

And here Ibn Kathir touches the nerve of it. He cites: "So think not that Allah will fail to keep His promise to His Messengers. Certainly, Allah is Almighty, All-Able of Retribution. On the Day when the earth will be changed to another earth and so will be the heavens, and they will appear before Allah, the One, the Irresistible" (14:47–48). The apparent delay is not neglect. A settlement postponed by Allah is not a settlement abandoned — and the verse describes the very earth and heavens being changed around the keeping of that promise.

Ayah 13 gives the one-line answer: **"For the Day of Decision."** Ibn Kathir's text renders it "the Day of Sorting Out," and glosses what is sorted: the men of Paradise from the men destined for Hell. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the Day of Decision, and describes it as "the great and horrible day." Both renderings hold the same idea — one thing cut cleanly away from another, and the matter settled.

## Ayah 14: "And what will make you realize?"

**"And what will make you realize what the Day of Decision is?"** Ibn Kathir says Allah asks this "in magnifying its matter." The question is not seeking information. It is a way of saying: you have just been given a name for this Day, and you must not mistake the name for the thing. Whatever you are now picturing falls short.

This is worth pausing over, because the passage has just handed us four enormous images. Ayah 14 says even those images do not exhaust it.

## Ayah 15: the verdict

**"Woe on that Day to the deniers!"** Ibn Kathir's gloss is that this is "woe unto them from Allah's torment that is coming in the future."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word *wail* means "destruction," and adds that according to certain hadith narratives, *wail* is a valley of Hell where the pus of the wounds of the inmates of Hell will be collected — and that this is the place where the deniers will live. (Maʿārif attributes this to hadith narratives in general without naming a collection, so it is best held exactly that loosely.)

Note carefully who the ayah names. Not the ignorant, not the weak, not simply the sinner — **al-mukadhdhibīn**. Ibn Kathir's text glosses them as the deniers of the Day of Resurrection; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the day of destruction "for the deniers and rejecters." This is the person who heard the promise of ayah 7 and answered that it will not happen. The whole passage has been an argument aimed precisely at him: here is what is coming, here is the Day it is set for, here is what that Day is called — and here is what it means for you to have called it a lie.

## Where this sūrah was given

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this sūrah with reports that put a frame around these lines.

Al-Bukhari recorded from ʿAbdullah — that is, Ibn Masʿūd — that he said: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a cave at Minā, *By the Mursalāt* was revealed to him. He was reciting it and I was learning it from his mouth. Verily, his mouth was moist with it when a snake leaped out at us." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Kill it!" They quickly went after it, but it got away. Then the Prophet ﷺ said, "It was saved from your harm just as you all were saved from its harm." Muslim also recorded this hadith by way of Al-Aʿmash. So these ayat about the sky splitting open were first heard by human ears inside a cave, learned syllable by syllable from a mouth still moist with the words.

Ibn Kathir then gives two further reports about this sūrah in the Maghrib prayer, and they are distinct:

- **Imam Ahmad** recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, who reported from his mother, that *she heard the Prophet ﷺ* reciting *By the Mursalāt* in the Maghrib prayer.
- **In a report from Mālik**, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: Umm Al-Faḍl (his mother) heard *him* — Ibn ʿAbbas — reciting *By the Mursalāt ʿUrfā*, so she said, "O my son! You reminded me with your recitation of this sūrah. Verily, it is the last thing I heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He recited it in the Maghrib prayer." Ibn Kathir notes that both Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded **this** report in the Two Sahihs by way of Mālik.

A sūrah that opens in a cave at Minā and is remembered as the last thing heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Maghrib is not a marginal one.

## Living it

**Take the delay for what it is.** The one honest question a denier could raise — *if it is so certain, where is it?* — is answered in ayah 12. The delay is a set term, not an absence. Ibn Kathir's citation of 14:47 is the point to hold onto: do not think that Allah will fail to keep His promise to His Messengers.

**Let the flatness of that ground do its work.** Ayah 10 removes the mountains so that no sight or trace of them remains; 18:47 shows the earth left as a leveled plain with not one person left behind. The same moment that clears the landscape is the moment that gathers everyone onto it.

**Check which side of ayah 15 you stand on.** Denial is not only a spoken creed. To live entirely as though the Day of Decision will never arrive is to say with one's life what the *mukadhdhib* says with his tongue. Reading ayat 8–14 slowly, and then hearing ayah 15, is meant to make a person feel that difference before the Day makes it for him.

passages.title: Earlier deniers destroyed, later ones to follow
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath:** Allah points the deniers back to history — *did We not destroy the earlier ones?* — then tells them that the same road is still open, and that later deniers will be sent down it after the first. Ayat 16–19 are one movement: a question about the past (16), a statement about what is still to come (17), the rule that joins the two (18), and the cry of woe that turns the hearer's attention from ruin already fallen to "that Day" still ahead (19).

## Ayah 16 — a question that is really evidence

**أَلَمْ نُهْلِكِ الْأَوَّلِينَ — "Did We not destroy earlier disbelievers?"**

Allah puts it as a question rather than a statement. And Ibn Kathir — the classical commentator whose tafsir is one of the most widely used — gathers this verse together with the verses that follow it under a single heading: **"The Call to contemplate the various Manifestations of Allah's Power."** So this is not a lecture delivered at the deniers. It is a summons to look, and the first thing they are made to look at is what already happened to people who stood where they are standing.

**Who are "the earlier ones"?** Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise: **"those who rejected the Messengers and opposed what they came to them with."** The category is not defined by era or ethnicity but by a stance — a messenger came, and they refused him and set themselves against what he brought.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — a detailed twentieth-century commentary — puts names to them: **the nations of ʿĀd, Thamūd, the nation of Lūṭ (peace be upon him), and Firʿawn (Pharaoh)**, and gives the reason they were destroyed in a single word: they were destroyed **because of their obstinacy.**

That word carries the weight of the verse. They were not destroyed for ignorance, or for weakness, or for a sin they were struggling against. Obstinacy is knowing and refusing anyway.

## Ayah 17 — "And We will make the later disbelievers follow them"

**ثُمَّ نُتْبِعُهُمُ الْآخِرِينَ**

Notice how the two verses sit against each other in the wording our sources give. Ayah 16 looks back — *did We not destroy* — and ayah 17 looks forward: *We will make the later disbelievers follow them.* Ibn Kathir renders it, **"So shall We make later generations to follow them."** The later deniers are not simply punished; they are made to come along behind the earlier ones, into the same end.

**What makes them "the later ones"?** Ibn Kathir answers in a phrase: **"from those who are similar to them."** The link between the destroyed ancients and the deniers of a later century is not lineage, not geography, not era — it is *resemblance*. Whoever takes up the same posture toward a messenger joins the same file. Time does not exempt you from a law; it only decides where in the line you stand.

### Maʿārif ul Qurʼān on how this ummah's deniers are dealt with

This is the passage's richest point, and it is easy to read past.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that **according to the popular reading**, ayah 17 means that **the present-day infidels, the people of Makkah, will receive punishment soon** — and it records that **they were punished and destroyed by Muslims in the Battle of Badr and so on.**

But then Maʿārif draws a distinction that changes how the whole warning reads. **The earlier nations and the deniers within this ummah — the community of the Prophet ﷺ — are not dealt with in the same way:**

- **The former nations** used to be destroyed by **celestial punishment** — a calamity sent down from the sky — and it took **all their habitations** with it.
- **The infidels in the community of the Holy Prophet ﷺ do not receive celestial punishment**, and Maʿārif states the reason plainly: **because of the Holy Prophet's ﷺ special honour.**
- Instead, **they are punished by the weapons of Muslims** — through events within history rather than by a calamity descending on them from above.
- And **the destruction is not general.** It does not sweep everyone away. **Only the obdurate criminal leaders are destroyed.**

So even the threat has a mercy folded inside it. The sentence still falls, but it falls narrowly, and it falls on the men who hardened themselves rather than on every roof in the town. The honour of the Prophet ﷺ is doing quiet work in the background of a verse about doom.

## Ayah 18 — the rule, stated flat

**كَذَٰلِكَ نَفْعَلُ بِالْمُجْرِمِينَ — "This is how We deal with the wicked."**

Ibn Kathir's rendering is **"Thus do We deal with the criminals"** — the "thus" pointing back at everything just described. And notice that both renderings state it as a standing practice, *this is how We deal*, not as a report of one closed incident. What happened to ʿĀd and Thamūd was not an exception in the record. It *is* the record.

Ibn Kathir quotes ayat 18 and 19 together as the conclusion that follows from 16 and 17 — *"Thus do We deal with the criminals. Woe that Day to the deniers!"* — and credits this reading of how the verses join to an earlier authority, noting simply: **"Ibn Jarir said this."**

The word rendered here as **"the wicked"** and by Ibn Kathir as **"the criminals"** describes people by what they have done. That lines up exactly with what Maʿārif said a verse earlier: what is destroyed is **the obdurate criminal leadership**, not a population. Allah's dealings here are with the guilty as guilty.

There is a mercy hidden in the very flatness of the statement. A rule you can read is a rule you can step out of. Nobody in ayah 18 is trapped by birth or by name: the verse describes conduct, and conduct can be abandoned.

## Ayah 19 — "Woe on that Day to the deniers!"

**وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلْمُكَذِّبِينَ**

This line is the sūrah's refrain, and it returns again later in the sūrah after further signs have been set out. Here it lands as the seal on everything from ayah 16 onward.

**Notice the timing.** Ayat 16–18 spoke of ruin that fell in this world — nations destroyed with all their habitations, leaders broken at Badr. Ayah 19 does not say "woe to them then." It says **"woe on that Day"** — a day still ahead of the one hearing the verse. So the worldly destruction was never the whole account. It stands in the record as a sample, published in history, while the reckoning itself keeps its own appointment.

**And who earns this woe?** The word is *the deniers*, and Ibn Kathir has already told us at ayah 16 who is meant by the destroyed: **"those who rejected the Messengers and opposed what they came to them with."** That is the shape of the denier throughout this passage. Not the man who was never told. The man who was told, and set himself against it.

## Living it

**Read history as evidence, not as entertainment.** Maʿārif names the nations ayah 16 is pointing at — ʿĀd, Thamūd, the nation of Lūṭ (peace be upon him), Firʿawn — and names what ruined them: obstinacy. Ayah 16 does not ask you to acquire new information. It asks you to let information you already hold press on you.

**Watch the trait, not the label.** Ibn Kathir's "from those who are similar to them" and ayah 18's "the wicked" both identify people by what they do. Obstinacy is a temperature a believer can check in himself: when a correction comes, when a clear proof arrives, does something in me dig in?

**Take the refrain personally, not tribally.** It is easy to hear "woe to the deniers" and immediately picture someone else. The sūrah repeats it deliberately, again and again after fresh signs, and the right response is not to identify the deniers but to make sure you are not standing among them.

**And hear the mercy inside the threat.** Maʿārif's note is worth keeping close: for this ummah, ruin is not poured indiscriminately from the sky, and that restraint is owed to the special honour of the Prophet ﷺ. Belonging to his community is itself a shelter — and a reason to be ashamed of squandering it.

passages.title: Created from a humble fluid, perfectly ordained
passages.tafsir:
**The turn from ruined nations to your own body.** In ayat 20–24 the surah takes its argument out of the graveyards of vanished peoples and puts it inside the listener himself. Having just recalled that earlier deniers were destroyed and that later ones will follow them (ayat 16–19), Allah asks a question nobody can answer with a "no": *Did We not create you from a humble fluid?* These five ayat run as one chain — the fluid (20), the secure place it is lodged in (21), the fixed term it is kept there for (22), the measuring of the whole process (23) — and then the refrain (24).

Ibn Kathir heads this section "The Call to contemplate the various Manifestations of Allah's Power," and he states its logic in a single sentence: here Allah is "reminding His creatures of His favor, and using the beginning of creation to support the idea of repeating it." That is the key to the passage. Every detail in these ayat does two jobs at once. It is a favour to be grateful for, and it is a proof that bringing you back after death is nothing difficult for the One who brought you here the first time.

## Where the argument is coming from

Ibn Kathir explains ayah 16, *Did We not destroy the ancients?*, as referring to "those who rejected the Messengers and opposed what they came to them with," and ayah 17, *then We will cause the later ones to follow them*, as meaning "those who are similar to them." He then quotes ayat 18 and 19 together — *Thus do We deal with the criminals. Woe that Day to the deniers!* — and adds, "Ibn Jarir said this," naming the earlier authority he is drawing the comment from.

And it is exactly at that point that Ibn Kathir marks the turn: "Then Allah, reminding His creatures of His favor, and using the beginning of creation to support the idea of repeating it, He says: *Did We not create you from a despised water?*" So the passage moves from a warning about how Allah deals with deniers straight into a reminder of how He deals with every human being at the very start of his existence. The Allah who ends nations is the Allah who assembled you in a womb.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a historical note on "the later ones" in ayah 17. On the popular reading, it says, the ayah means that the deniers of that day, the people of Makkah, would be punished soon — and they were, "punished and destroyed by Muslims in the Battle of Badr and so on." Maʿārif then draws a distinction worth keeping in mind: the former nations "used to be destroyed by celestial punishment with all their habitations," whereas "the infidels in the community of the Holy Prophet ﷺ do not receive celestial punishment, because of the Holy Prophet's ﷺ special honour." Their punishment came instead through the weapons of the Muslims, and it was not indiscriminate — "the destruction is not general. Only the obdurate criminal leaders are destroyed." Even the threat here, on this reading, is bounded by the honour Allah gave His Messenger ﷺ.

## Ayah 20: a humble fluid — and whose weakness it proves

*Did We not create you from a humble fluid?* The Arabic word is **mahīn** — rendered "humble" in our translation and "despised" in Ibn Kathir's. It is important to hear what the comparison actually is. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "weak and despised **in comparison to the power of the Creator**." The point is not contempt for the human being. The point is the distance between the raw material and the result: a fluid too slight to impress anyone, and out of it a hearing, seeing, thinking, arguing person who has the nerve to doubt his Maker.

Ibn Kathir supports this with what "has been reported in the Hadith of Busr bin Jahhash," in which Allah says:

> "(O) Son of Adam! How can you think that I am unable, and yet I created you from something like this?"

— that is, from semen. Read that slowly, because it is the argument of the whole passage compressed into one line. The denier's real claim, underneath everything else, is that Allah cannot bring the dead back. The answer here is not a display of thunder but a pointing finger at the least impressive thing in the world: *that* is where you came from. A person who admits his own origin has already conceded the case.

## Ayah 21: placed in a secure lodging

*…placing it in a secure place.* Ibn Kathir explains: "We gathered him in the womb, where the fluid of the man and the woman settles. The womb has been prepared for this, as a protector of the fluid deposited in it."

Three things are packed into that comment.

**"We gathered him."** The verb is Allah's. The fluid does not find its way anywhere by itself; it is *placed*. And notice Ibn Kathir's own pronoun: the ayah says "We placed **it**," but he writes "We gathered **him**." The person is already in view, because that speck is you.

**"Where the fluid of the man and the woman settles."** Ibn Kathir reads the "secure place" as the meeting point of both — the place where what comes from the two of them comes to rest.

**"The womb has been prepared for this, as a protector."** The shelter was built before the guest arrived. This is why the ayah belongs in a list of *favours* and not only of *proofs*. Ibn Kathir has already told us Allah is here "reminding His creatures of His favor": the arrangement that kept you alive before anyone knew you existed was arranged for you in advance.

## Ayah 22: until an appointed time

*…until an appointed time.* Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "For a known period," and explains: "for a fixed period of time, which is from six months to nine months." He is giving the outer limits within which pregnancies run. The weight of the ayah is in the word *known*: the term is not an accident of biology that happens to land somewhere, it is a period fixed and known — which is precisely what the next ayah goes on to say.

## Ayah 23: the measuring, and the Measurer

*We perfectly ordained its development. How excellent are…* — Ibn Kathir renders the same ayah, **fa-qadarnā fa-niʿma al-qādirūn**, as "So We did measure; and We are the best to measure."

Everything the ayat have just described — the fluid, the lodging, the timing — is gathered up in that one statement. The known term did not simply turn out that way; it was measured out. What looks from the inside like a natural process is, in the Qur'an's own account of it, a deliberate determination.

And then the ayah does something striking: it praises the measuring. *How excellent* — "We are the best to measure." This is one of those places where the Qur'an teaches us what to think of Allah by telling us what He says of His own work. The believer affirms this of Allah exactly as He affirmed it of Himself, really and truly — without imagining His measuring to be anything like the measuring of a creature, and without emptying the words of the meaning He gave them.

There is a quiet consolation buried here for anyone willing to take it. If the term of your first and most fragile confinement was measured out by the One who calls His own measuring the best, it is worth sitting with what that means for the terms you are living inside now.

## Ayah 24: the refrain, and who it lands on

*Woe on that Day to the deniers!*

The refrain is not new at ayah 24. It had already fallen at ayah 19, after the warning about the destroyed nations. Now it returns — this time after evidence drawn not from history but from the listener's own body. Nothing has been added to the warning; what has been added is the proof standing in front of it.

Ibn Kathir's own explanation of what the refrain means comes at its next recurrence, further on in this section of signs rather than at ayah 24 itself. But it tells us how he reads its force throughout: woe, he says, "to whoever reflects upon these created things which demonstrate the greatness of their Creator, then after that continues to reject Him and disbelieve in Him."

That reading changes who the ayah is aimed at. The "deniers" are not people who never heard. They are people who *looked*. They considered the created things in front of them, they saw the greatness those things point to, and they carried on denying anyway. The warning is against a very specific failure: knowing enough, and doing nothing with it.

## Living with these ayat

**Trace yourself backwards.** The passage does not ask you to accept an abstract doctrine; it asks you to remember a fact about your own body. Ibn Kathir's framing is worth making into a habit — reading the beginning of creation as support for the idea of its repetition. When resurrection feels implausible, the answer offered here is not new information but something you already grant: it has been done before, with you.

**Let it cure arrogance.** The hadith of Busr bin Jahhash addresses "son of Adam" directly, and the sting is in the contrast: how can you treat Allah as unable, when your own beginning was that? The same thought unmakes pride over lineage, wealth, or intellect. Everyone in the room came from the same humble fluid.

**Receive it as kindness, not only as an argument.** Ibn Kathir says Allah is here "reminding His creatures of His favor." A place of safety, prepared in advance, held for a known term. Gratitude for the sheltering you were given before you could ask for it is a right response to these ayat, and a truer one than intellectual assent alone.

**Do not let reflection stall short of submission.** By Ibn Kathir's reading of the refrain, contemplation that ends in admiration of the Creator's greatness and goes no further into obedience is precisely what earns the "woe."

passages.title: The earth as lodging for living and dead
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat ask you to look down at the ground you are standing on and see it as evidence. The earth, Allah says, was made a *kifāt* — a lodging, a receptacle that holds you on its surface while you live and takes you into itself when you die — and it was fitted with towering, firm mountains and supplied with fresh water. Ayah 28 then closes the section with the surah's recurring refrain: **Woe on that Day to the deniers!** What holds the four together is a single argument: a person who walks on this earth, is given this water, and is himself destined for this soil, and still denies the One who arranged it, has no excuse left.

## Ayah 25: the earth as *kifāt*

The commentary of Ibn Kathir on this stretch of the surah runs under the heading *"The Call to contemplate the various Manifestations of Allah's Power."* That is exactly what these ayat do. They come after a run of similar questions — *"Did We not destroy the ancients?"* (16), *"Did We not create you from a despised water?"* (20) — and Ibn Kathir names the purpose of the whole sequence in one sentence: Allah is *"reminding His creatures of His favor, and using the beginning of creation to support the idea of repeating it."* Each question is at once a gift you cannot deny and a proof of power you cannot dodge. Our ayah is put in the same form: **أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ** — *alam najʿal*, "Have We not made…?"

Everything in it turns on one word: **كِفَاتًا**, *kifāt*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the word back to its root: *kifāt* comes from *kaft*, which means **"to gather things together."** So a *kifāt*, the commentary says, is *"a thing that embodies many things within itself"* — a container into which scattered things are drawn in and kept. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah carries the same idea: *"Have We not made the earth Kifat — a receptacle?"*

Notice what that does to your sense of the ground. We think of the earth as a flat stage we happen to stand on. The word says it is a container, and we are its contents. Everything loose — every person, every generation — is gathered up and held by it.

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites each turn the word a slightly different way, and together they give you its range:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *"Kifat means a place of shelter."* The stress falls on refuge — the earth as the place that takes you in and keeps you.
- **Mujāhid** said: *"It holds the dead so that nothing is seen of it."* Here the stress falls on concealment: the earth receives what is buried in it and hides it from sight.
- **Ash-Shaʿbī** said: *"Its interior is for your dead and its surface is for your living."* Ibn Kathir notes that **Mujāhid and Qatādah also said this.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it as a matter of design: the earth is created by Allah *"in a fashion that humans when alive, remain on its back, and when dead, in its belly."*

## Ayah 26: "for the living and the dead"

Ayah 26 is only two words — **أَحْيَاءً وَأَمْوَاتًا**, *aḥyāʾan wa amwātā*, "for the living and the dead" — and they are what makes ayah 25 land. Note that the ayah does not say the earth gathers *life and death* as abstractions. It names **people**: living ones and dead ones. You are one of the two nouns in this ayah, and you will move from the first to the second.

So the earth performs two opposite services with the same body of soil. Its **back** carries you: it is where you walk, farm, build, marry, argue, pray. Its **belly** receives you: it is where you are laid and covered. One single creation, doing both jobs. This is why *kifāt* is such an exact word — the same receptacle has an outside and an inside, and each of us is assigned to both in turn.

There is a mercy in this that we rarely stop to feel. Mujāhid's phrase — *nothing is seen of it* — describes a covering extended to a body that can no longer cover itself; the ground was made able to do that.

There is also a warning in it. The refrain in ayah 28 is aimed at the deniers. To them the passage quietly says: the earth is not your final address. You are on its surface for a term, then in its interior. As Ibn Kathir framed the whole sequence, Allah is using the beginning of creation to establish that He can repeat it — the One who gathered you in the womb *"for a fixed period of time"* has also arranged where you are gathered afterwards.

Ibn Kathir also brings in here, in commenting on the despised water of ayah 20, a hadith reported from Busr bin Jahhash in which Allah says: *"(O) Son of Adam! How can you think that I am unable, and yet I created you from something like this?"* — that is, from semen. (The commentary quotes it without naming a collection, so we pass on the teaching without attributing it to one.) The whole passage speaks in that voice. Look at where you came from, and at where you are kept — then tell Me what I cannot do.

## Ayah 27: the mountains, and the fresh water

Ayah 27 keeps the same "Have We not…?" pressure and adds two more items to the list.

**وَجَعَلْنَا فِيهَا رَوَاسِيَ شَامِخَاتٍ** — *"and placed upon it towering, firm mountains,"* rendered by Ibn Kathir as *"And have placed therein fixed towers."* His gloss is simple: **the mountains.** And their function, he says, is that *"the earth is held in place with them so that it does not shake and sway."* Follow the argument: the receptacle that holds you needs to be steady, or it is no shelter at all. So the same Lord who made it a *kifāt* also stabilised it.

**وَأَسْقَيْنَاكُمْ مَاءً فُرَاتًا** — *"and given you fresh [water]"*; Ibn Kathir renders it *"and have given you Furat water."* **Furāt** he explains as *"cold and delicious water."* And he points to its two supplies: it comes *"from the clouds, or from what He causes to gush forth from the springs of the earth."* Rain from above; springs from below. Both arrive without you arranging them.

Look at how the two clauses are worded. Not "mountains exist" and "water exists," but **We placed** and **We have given you**. The mountains are placed *in it*, the ground you were just told is your container; the water is given *to you*, with you as the one served. The favour is named as a favour, and the Giver is named as the Giver.

## Ayah 28: the refrain, and who it is for

**وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ** — *"Woe on that Day to the deniers!"* The same line closes ayah 19 and ayah 24, and it closes our passage in ayah 28. It returns after each stretch of evidence: the proof is laid out, and then the verdict on anyone who shrugs at it.

Ibn Kathir's gloss on this occurrence is precise and worth reading slowly. Woe, he says, *"to whoever reflects upon these created things which demonstrate the greatness of their Creator, then after that continues to reject Him and disbelieve in Him."*

That is a specific charge. It is aimed at the one who *did* look — who considered the ground that shelters him, the mountains that steady it, the water given to him — registered the greatness behind it, and then went on denying anyway. The passage has just walked such a person through the evidence item by item; ayah 28 is the bill.

Note also **يَوْمَئِذٍ**, *yawma'idhin*, "on that Day." The woe is not announced for today. Denial is comfortable now. The verse tells you exactly when the reckoning for it arrives.

## Living it

**Let the ground preach to you.** The framing here is *contemplation* — that these created things "demonstrate the greatness of their Creator." A step on solid ground, a mountain on the horizon, a cup of cold water: the passage treats each as an argument, not as scenery.

**Remember which side of the earth you are on.** Ash-Shaʿbī's sentence is worth memorising: *its interior is for your dead and its surface is for your living*. You are currently on the back of the receptacle. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the move from its back to its belly as simply how the earth was made for us — not a possibility, but the design.

**Take the gifts as gifts, not as facts.** Mountains that hold the earth from shaking, and water that arrives cold and delicious from cloud and spring, are described here in the language of favour — *We placed*, *We have given you*. The believer's response to ordinary stability and ordinary water is gratitude, because the passage presents them as things given, not things owed.

**Do not be the person in ayah 28.** The most sobering line in this whole section is Ibn Kathir's: the one condemned is the one who reflected, saw the greatness, and rejected anyway. Reflection that does not change how you live is not a neutral outcome — this passage treats it as the very thing that seals the case against you.

passages.title: Driven into the fire's three-columned smoke
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath.** These six ayat are the sentence being carried out. Ibn Kathir heads this section "The driving of the Criminals to their Final Abode in Hell and how it will be done" — and that is exactly the movement: an order to march (ayat 29–30), a description of what they are marching into (ayat 30–33), and the verdict that seals it (ayah 34). What binds them into one unit is a single terrible irony: the thing they spent their lives calling a lie has become the destination they are commanded to walk into.

## "Proceed to the very thing you called a lie" (ayah 29)

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: "Allah informs about the disbelievers who deny the final abode, the recompense, Paradise, and the Hellfire. On the Day of Judgement it will be said to them" — and then comes the command.

Notice what ayah 29 does *not* say. It does not say "Proceed to the Fire." It names the destination only by their own relationship to it: **مَا كُنتُم بِهِۦ تُكَذِّبُونَ** — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "that which you used to deny." The Fire is identified by the very word they used to dismiss it. Their denial has become its address.

And the command itself comes twice. Ibn Kathir quotes the two ayat together, and the same word opens both: "Depart you to that which you used to deny! Depart you to a shadow in three columns." The passage moves them along, one push after another.

## The shade that gives no shade (ayat 30–31)

Ayah 30 sends them **إِلَىٰ ظِلّٖ ذِي ثَلَٰثِ شُعَبٖ** — "to a shadow in three columns."

Hold on that word: *shade*. The ayah names it — and ayah 31 takes it back at once: **لَّا ظَلِيلٖ**, "neither shady." The relief is offered and cancelled in the same breath.

What is this shade, then? Ibn Kathir explains: "a flame of fire when it rises and ascends with smoke. So due to its severity and strength, it will have three columns." So the "shade" is the pall of smoke thrown up by the flame — and the three columns are put down by Ibn Kathir to the fire's own severity and strength.

Ayah 31 then closes both doors at once. Ibn Kathir: it is "shade of the smoke that comes from the flame – which itself will not have a shade, nor will it benefit against the flame. This means it will not protect them from the heat of the flame." Read that slowly. It is a shade that has no shade of its own. Not only does it fail to cool; it fails to shield. The one thing on that plain that looks like shelter turns out to be produced *by* the very fire it appears to shelter from.

## Sparks like castles, sparks like camels (ayat 32–33)

Having described the smoke, Allah turns to what the Fire throws off. **إِنَّهَا تَرۡمِي بِشَرَرٖ كَٱلۡقَصۡرِ** — "Verily, it throws sparks as *Al-Qaṣr*."

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* gives the plain lexical sense: *qaṣr* means "a huge, magnificent castle." Ibn Kathir agrees on the force of the image: "its sparks will shoot out from its flame like huge castles." A spark is the smallest thing a fire throws off. Here the smallest offcut of this Fire is the size of a fortress. If that is the spark, the mind is left to reckon with the blaze.

**Where the scholars read *al-qaṣr* differently.** Ibn Kathir records two lines of interpretation, and it is worth having both:

- **Buildings.** Ibn Masʿūd said, "Like forts."
- **Timber.** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and Mālik who reported from Zayd bin Aslam and others said, "This means the trunk of trees."

Imam Al-Bukhari recorded the ground of the second reading, from Ibn ʿAbbās himself: "We were directed to the timber a length of three cubits or more in order to use it for construction of buildings. We used to call it *Al-Qaṣr*." (This is Ibn ʿAbbās explaining a usage of the word, not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ.) So in their speech the word could carry a builder's meaning: great baulks of construction timber. Either way the comparison holds — something massive and heavy, thrown through the air like nothing.

Then ayah 33: **كَأَنَّهُۥ جِمَٰلَتٞ صُفۡرٞ**. *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* unpacks the vocabulary: *jimālah* is used in the sense of *jamal*, and means "camel"; and *ṣufr* is the plural of *aṣfar*, which means "yellow."

*Maʿārif* also reads the two similes as a sequence rather than a repetition — one picture in two stages. The Fire "will emit such huge sparks of fire, as if they were huge and magnificent castles. Then they will break up into little splinters, as if they were yellowish camels." First the scale of a fortress hurled upward; then the breaking apart into smaller bodies scattering across the sky.

**Where the scholars read *ṣufr* differently.** Ibn Kathir again gives two views:

- **Black camels.** *Ṣufr* camels "means, black camels." This is the view of Mujāhid, Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn Jarīr favoured it.
- **Ropes of ships.** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr said of *jimālat ṣufr*: "Meaning ropes of ships." And in the report Imam Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās: "These (*Jimālāt*) are ropes of ships that are bundled until they resemble the intestines of men."

Ibn Kathir names Mujāhid among those reported for each of these readings.

On the colour, *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* offers a reconciliation, citing *Rūḥ*: *ṣufr* means yellow, and "some scholars have translated the word *ṣufr* as 'black' because yellowish colour of camels tends to blackness." So the two renderings are not as far apart as they look; one shades into the other.

## "Woe that Day to the deniers" (ayah 34)

And then the refrain falls: **وَيۡلٞ يَوۡمَئِذٖ لِّلۡمُكَذِّبِينَ** — "Woe that Day to the deniers." Ibn Kathir's rendering adds who is meant: the deniers "of the Day of Resurrection."

Read it against ayah 29 and the passage closes like a circle. In ayah 29 they are addressed by what they did: "that which you used to deny." In ayah 34 they are named for it: "the deniers." Denial was their act; now it is simply what they are called. Nothing else about them is mentioned — not their wealth, not their lineage, not their arguments. One act has become their whole name.

And Ibn Kathir has already told us at the head of his commentary what it was they denied: "the final abode, the recompense, Paradise, and the Hellfire." The refrain then returns again at ayah 37 and ayah 40 — Allah lets each new stretch of the Day's horror finish, then stamps it with the same line.

## Living it

The sources here are describing, not legislating, so the lesson has to stay close to the text — and the text is aimed at one thing: denial, calling the truth a lie. Everything in the passage grows out of it. The sentence in ayah 29 is worded from it; the verdict in ayah 34 is named after it.

Two things worth sitting with.

**First: the destination is described as something they already chose.** Ayah 29 sends them toward "that which you used to deny" — as though the Fire were simply the place their own denial had always been walking. Belief in the Last Day is not an abstract item of doctrine; the Qur'an here treats it as a direction of travel.

**Second: the shelter that is not a shelter.** Ayah 31 is the quietest and most devastating line in the passage. There is a "shade" there — and by Ibn Kathir's explanation it has no shade of its own and does not benefit against the flame at all. Whatever a person leans on that has no power to shield them from Allah's decree is exactly that: a shade that gives no shade. Better to discover that now, while the discovery costs nothing.

And there is a mercy folded into all of it: this description is being read out **in advance**. Those in ayah 34 receive the woe; whoever hears these words today is still on the other side of that Day, and still able to answer them.

passages.title: The deniers silenced and left without escape
passages.tafsir:
**In brief.** These six ayat show the deniers standing in the court of the Last Day with nothing left to say. First their tongues are stopped (35) and permission to make excuses is withheld (36); then they are told what Day this actually is — the Day of Decision, with them and the men of old brought together on one common plane (38); and finally they are challenged to use any plot they think might save them (39). What holds the passage together is a single movement: every avenue of escape a human being normally reaches for — words, excuses, numbers, cleverness — is closed off one after another, and after each closure the refrain falls like a gavel: **"Woe on that Day to the deniers!"** (37, 40).

## Where we are in the sūrah

Immediately before this, in ayat 29–34, the deniers are being driven to their destination: *"Depart you to that which you used to deny! Depart you to a shadow in three columns"* — which Ibn Kathir explains as *"a flame of fire when it rises and ascends with smoke. So due to its severity and strength, it will have three columns."* It is a shade that is *"neither shady nor of any use against the fierce flame of the Fire"* — Ibn Kathir: it *"will not protect them from the heat of the flame."* The sparks it throws are like *al-Qaṣr* — *"like huge castles"*; Ibn Masʿūd said, "Like forts"; Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and Mālik reporting from Zayd bin Aslam and others said, "This means the trunk of trees."

So the scene is already set: the condemned are on their way. Our passage is what happens in the courtroom itself — Ibn Kathir titles this section *"The Inability of the Criminals to speak, make Excuses, or step forward on the Day of Judgement."*

## Ayah 35 — a Day when they do not speak

**هَٰذَا يَوْمُ لَا يَنطِقُونَ** — *"That will be a Day when they shall not speak."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss here is stark in its brevity: *"meaning, they will not speak."* There is nothing to soften and nothing to add. The very tool with which these people had denied the warning simply fails them.

It is worth noticing that ayah 35 and ayah 38 open with the same word — **هَٰذَا**, *"This is a Day..."* — which binds the two halves of the passage together: this is a Day they do not speak; this is the Day of Decision.

## Ayah 36 — and no permission to excuse themselves

**وَلَا يُؤْذَنُ لَهُمْ فَيَعْتَذِرُونَ** — *"And they will not be permitted to put forth any excuse."*

Ayah 35 removes the ability; ayah 36 removes the permission. Ibn Kathir puts both together: *"they will not be able to speak, nor will they be granted permission to speak so that they can make excuses."*

Read that sentence slowly and its structure does the work. Permission is *granted* — it is not something a person seizes for himself, it comes from above, and here it is withheld. And the excusing is downstream of it: permission to speak *"so that they can make excuses."* Cut the permission and the excuse never comes into existence.

That is precisely how Ibn Kathir continues: *"Rather, the proof will be established against them, and they will be called upon to speak about the wrong that they did, but they will not be able to say anything."* Note the awful detail — they *are* called upon. The invitation to answer is extended, and the answer does not come. And note what has already happened before they are called: *the proof has been established.* A man who is merely silenced might still be innocent; here the case is closed before the question is put.

## "But doesn't the Qur'an say they will speak?"

This is the question a careful reader will hit at once, and both of our commentaries take it up.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: *"other verses of the Qur'an inform us that they will speak and will be permitted to offer excuses."* Its answer, citing *Rūḥ*: **there is no discrepancy between the two verses, "because there will be various stages on the Plain of Gathering (Mahshar) through which people will have to pass. Sometimes they will pass through a stage where it would be forbidden for them to speak or offer excuses; and at another stage they will be permitted."**

Ibn Kathir says the same thing in his own words: *"The courts of the Day of Judgement will occur in stages. Sometimes the Lord informs of this stage and sometimes He informs of that stage. This is to show the terrors and calamities of that Day."* The very rendering of the ayah carried in his text makes the point in a parenthesis: *"That will be a Day when they shall not speak (during some part of it)."*

Two things are worth drawing out of this:

**First, a principle for reading the Qur'an.** Two verses that appear to collide are often two windows onto one long event at different moments. The Day of Judgement, on this explanation, is not an instant; it is a proceeding with stages, and different passages report different stages. And this is not a patch invented to close a hole — it is the answer the classical mufassirūn themselves give here.

**Second, why Allah discloses it this way.** Ibn Kathir's reason is worth sitting with: the varied reports exist *"to show the terrors and calamities of that Day."* We are not being given a transcript to satisfy curiosity. We are being shown, from angle after angle, what it is like to stand there — and one of those angles is the horror of being unable to get a single word out.

## Ayat 37 and 40 — the refrain

**وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلْمُكَذِّبِينَ** — *"Woe on that Day to the deniers!"*

The refrain lands twice in this short passage: once after the silencing (37) and once after the challenge (40). Ibn Kathir marks its placement — *"Thus, after all the details of this discussion, He says: Woe that Day to the deniers!"* Each time the Qur'an finishes drawing a scene, it turns from the scene and names who it is for.

And it names them by their act, not merely as disbelievers but as **the deniers**. Ibn Kathir opens this whole passage by identifying them exactly so: *"Allah informs about the disbelievers who deny the final abode, the recompense, Paradise, and the Hellfire."* It was the same word that sent them off in ayah 29 — *"Depart you to that which you used to **deny**."* Those named for their denial are the ones who, on that Day, will not speak.

## Ayah 38 — the Day of Decision, and the men of old

**هَٰذَا يَوْمُ ٱلْفَصْلِ ۖ جَمَعْنَٰكُمْ وَٱلْأَوَّلِينَ** — *"That will be a Day of Decision! We have brought you and the men of old together!"* The translation given with the ayah renders it *"the Day of ˹Final˺ Decision."*

And the decision is handed down in front of everyone. Ibn Kathir explains: *"He will gather all of them by His power on one common plane, He will make them hear the caller and He will cause them to see."*

Three points in that one sentence deserve attention:

- **"By His power."** Gathering all of them is presented as a matter of Allah's power — the same power that, in the next ayah, cannot be escaped. We affirm this of Allah as it is stated, as the Salaf did, without asking how, without likening it to anything in creation, and without reducing it to a figure of speech.
- **"He will make them hear the caller."** In an assembly of that magnitude, one call reaches every ear.
- **"He will cause them to see."** They will not merely be told what is happening. They will see it.

And there is something quietly devastating in *"you **and** the men of old."* The earlier generations are not somewhere else, in some other reckoning. Ibn Kathir's phrase is *"on one common plane"* — the same ground, the same Day, the same court.

## Ayah 39 — "So, if you have a plot, use it against Me"

**فَإِن كَانَ لَكُمْ كَيْدٌ فَكِيدُونِ** — *"So, if you have a plot, use it against Me!"* The translation given with the ayah renders *kayd* as *"a scheme ˹to save yourselves˺."*

Ibn Kathir notes what is most striking about this ayah before he explains it: *"This is an address from the Creator to His servants."* The Lord of the worlds speaks to them directly, in the first person, and dares them.

The ayah grants them the premise for the sake of argument — *"if you have a plot"* — and then names the target: *fa-kīdūni*, "then use it against **Me**." Ibn Kathir calls this *"a serious threat and a harsh warning"* and unpacks it as: *"if you are able to save yourselves from being seized by Me, and rescue yourselves from My ruling, then do so. But you are certainly not able to do so."* It has the form of a command and the force of an exposure. Like a captor saying "go on, then" to a prisoner in chains, the invitation is itself the proof of helplessness.

He then places the ayah alongside two others. From Sūrah ar-Raḥmān: *"O assembly of Jinn and men! If you have power to pass beyond the zones of the heavens and the earth, then pass beyond (them)! But you will never be able to pass them, except with authority (from Allah)!"* (55:33) — the same shape exactly, a challenge issued and refuted in a single breath. And: *"And you will not harm Him in the least"* (11:57).

Finally Ibn Kathir cites a hadith in which the words are Allah's own. His text introduces it simply as *"It is narrated in a Hadith (that Allah said)"* — without naming a collection, so no collection is named here either: **"O My servants! You all can never attain My benefit and thereby benefit Me, and you all can never attain My harm and thereby harm Me."**

That report reframes the whole challenge. Allah is not defending Himself against a real threat when He says *"use it against Me."* Nothing the creation does reaches Him — not its benefit and not its harm. The challenge exists entirely for the sake of the ones being challenged: to strip away, in the moment when it matters most, the illusion of leverage they had lived by.

## Living it

The passage is not primarily about the deniers of the past; it is aimed at whoever is reading it now. A few things it presses on us:

**Every excuse has a deadline.** The human instinct under accusation is to explain — *I didn't know, I was busy, everyone else was doing it, I meant to.* Ayah 36 shows a court where that instinct meets a closed door: no permission granted, so no excuse offered. Whatever needs to be settled with Allah, the time to speak is while speech is still granted.

**The case is already complete.** Ibn Kathir's phrase — *"the proof will be established against them"* — means nothing is uncovered on that Day that was not already true.

**Numbers and heritage are not a defence.** Ayah 38 brings "you and the men of old" together on one common plane. No one is standing somewhere quieter.

**No plot survives the Day of Decision.** Ayah 39 is the end of self-reliance: *"But you are certainly not able to do so."* The only thing that will help is what a person sent ahead — and the mercy of the One who is issuing the challenge.

And notice, running underneath all of it, that these six ayat are a warning given **in advance**. They describe a silence in order that we might use our voices now, while asking, repenting, and affirming the truth still count for something.

passages.title: The righteous amid shade, springs, and fruit
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Mursalāt has been speaking of the wretched. Now it turns its face to the other side. Ayat 41–44 open on the people of taqwa — shade, springs, fruit, and a spoken welcome — and then ayah 45 brings back the surah's recurring refrain: **woe that Day to the deniers.** These five ayat are best taken as one picture with a caption underneath it: here is what those who feared Allah are given, and here is what the deniers threw away.

## A shade set against a shade

The first thing to notice about ayah 41 is that it is an answer. Ibn Kathir reads it against what the surah has already said about the wretched, who "will be in shades of *Al-Yahmum*, which is purtrid, black smoke." So when Allah says that those with taqwa are **فِي ظِلَالٍ وَعُيُونٍ** — "amidst shades and springs" — the very same word covers both parties, and the contrast is the point. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: the people of taqwa "will be in the opposite condition of the wretched people."

Both groups end up under a shade. One shade is choking smoke that no one would ever call shelter; the other is the cool overhang of a garden. The description of Paradise here is not left standing on its own — it is laid directly over the image of the Fire, so that you feel the difference rather than merely learn it.

Both nouns in ayah 41 are plural: *ẓilāl*, shades, not one shade; and *ʿuyūn*, springs, not one spring. And notice how Ibn Kathir paraphrases: he says they "will be in gardens and springs on the Day of Judgement." He moves from *shades* to *gardens* without a pause, and that tells you what kind of shade is meant. Not an empty patch of shadow — the shade of a garden, with running springs in it.

## Who exactly are "the righteous"?

Ayah 41 does not begin with a vague word for good people. It says **الْمُتَّقِينَ**, *al-muttaqīn* — those who have *taqwa*. Taqwa is often rendered as mindfulness of Allah, or fear of Him; Ibn Kathir gives it here in its most practical, unromantic form. These are Allah's servants "who have Taqwa and worship Him by performing the obligations and abandoning the forbidden things."

That is worth sitting with, because it is a definition anyone can act on today. Taqwa in this ayah is not a mood or a pitch of spiritual intensity. It is two concrete movements: **do what He has made obligatory, and stay away from what He has forbidden.** The one who lives between those two lines is the one described here, resting in shade beside springs.

## The table: fruit they desire, and a word spoken in kindness

Ayah 42 adds: **وَفَوَاكِهَ مِمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ** — "and fruits, such as they desire." Again the plural: *fawākih*, fruits, of many kinds. Ibn Kathir explains: "and from other types of fruits, they will have whatever they request."

Two things are promised at once, and they are not the same thing. The first is *abundance* — there is fruit, and there is variety. The second, and the sweeter of the two, is *correspondence*: the fruit matches the desire. In this world the gap between what we want and what is actually available is a permanent, low-grade ache. There, that gap simply closes. Ibn Kathir's word "request" is telling — the wanting itself is honoured, not merely tolerated. And notice what the description does not mention: no price, no labour, no scarcity, no season that ends.

Then ayah 43 stops describing and starts speaking: **كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا هَنِيئًا بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ** — "Eat and drink comfortably for that which you used to do."

Ibn Kathir's comment on this is short, and worth quoting exactly: "this will be said to them out of kindness for them." That one remark changes how the ayah sounds. It is not an instruction they needed, as though they were standing awkwardly beside the food waiting for permission. It is the language of a generous host — *go on, eat, enjoy it, it is yours.* Part of the honour is simply in being addressed at all. The word *hanī'an* is what the translators are reaching for with "comfortably" and "happily"; set that beside the earthly experience of eating and drinking, where pleasure is so often shadowed by what follows.

And then the tail of the ayah: **بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ** — "for that which you used to do." The invitation is tied to deeds already behind them. The passage draws a straight line from what they did, back then, to this table.

## From a scene to a rule

**إِنَّا كَذَٰلِكَ نَجْزِي الْمُحْسِنِينَ** — "Verily, thus We reward the *muḥsinīn*." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as "this is Our reward for whoever does good deeds," and he notes that with this ayah Allah is "reestablishing what He has previously mentioned."

That is precisely the function of ayah 44. Ayat 41–43 showed you particular people in a particular garden; ayah 44 pulls back and states the principle behind the scene. This is not a one-off favour granted to a select few. It is how Allah deals with the *muḥsinīn* — the doers of good — as a settled rule. Whoever enters that description enters that reward.

There is a quiet shift of vocabulary across the passage that repays attention. It opens with *al-muttaqīn* (ayah 41) and closes the description with *al-muḥsinīn* (ayah 44). Taqwa, as Ibn Kathir defined it, is the guarding — obligations fulfilled, the forbidden left alone. The *muḥsinīn*, as he defines them, are "whoever does good deeds." The same people are being named twice, from two angles: what they kept away from, and what they put in.

## And then the refrain

Without a pause: **وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلْمُكَذِّبِينَ** — "˹But˺ woe on that Day to the deniers!"

This refrain recurs through sūrah al-Mursalāt, but here it may be at its most piercing, precisely because of where it is placed. It does not follow a description of the Fire. It follows shade, springs, fruit, and a kind word from Allah. Read in its place, the woe is measured against what has just been shown: all of this was on offer, and they called it a lie. What is being pointed at is not only the punishment; it is the loss.

## Living it

Keep to the passage's own logic; it does not need stretching.

**Taqwa is defined for you here, so use the definition.** Ibn Kathir did not describe the people of ayah 41 as mystics or scholars. He described them as those who performed what Allah made obligatory and abandoned what He forbade. That is the road into this passage, and it is walkable today.

**Deeds are the currency.** Ayah 43 ties the eating and drinking of the Hereafter to "what you used to do." Take Ibn Kathir's two movements and picture them: the obligation carried out when nobody was watching; the forbidden thing walked away from when walking away cost you something. That is what the invitation in ayah 43 is answering.

**Let the contrast do its work.** Both groups in this surah end up under a shade — one of them the shade of black smoke, the other the shade of a garden with springs running through it. When ayah 45 says "woe that Day to the deniers," it is asking you — while there is still time — to make sure it is ayah 41 that describes you, and not ayah 45.

passages.title: The last warning to those who will not bow
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close Sūrah al-Mursalāt. Ibn Kathir identifies the audience precisely: ayah 46 "is an address to the deniers of the Day of Judgement." The passage takes them apart in three strokes — a bitter invitation to enjoy the little that is left (46), the refusal to bow that lies underneath the denial (48), and a final question that has no possible answer (50). Twice between them falls the refrain that has been sounding through the surah: *Woe on that Day to the deniers* (47, 49).

## Ayah 46: a command that is not a permission

**"Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while. Verily, you are criminals."**

Just before this passage, Allah describes those who had *taqwā* — Ibn Kathir explains them as His servants who "worship Him by performing the obligations and abandoning the forbidden things" — amidst shades and springs, with fruits "such as they desire," meaning, as Ibn Kathir says, "they will have whatever they request." Ibn Kathir notes the contrast built into that word *shade*: they are "in the opposite condition of the wretched people, who will be in shades of Al-Yahmum, which is putrid, black smoke." And to the people of *taqwā* it is said, *"Eat and drink comfortably for that which you used to do"* — words that, Ibn Kathir observes, "will be said to them out of kindness for them."

Ayah 46 opens with the very same verb, turned on the opposite party, and every trace of that kindness is gone. There is no "comfortably." There is no honoured record of deeds. Instead the sentence ends: **"Verily, you are criminals."**

Ibn Kathir names the device exactly: **"It is commanding them with a command of threat and intimidation."** So this is a command in grammar only. Its force is the reverse of permission — the form of an invitation used to deliver a threat, the way one might say to a man already sentenced, *go on, finish your meal.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Abū Ḥayyān, gives the substance plainly: "They may eat and drink and enjoy themselves in this world, but the span is short, and then there will be nothing but punishment for them." Maʿārif adds a detail about how the words reach them: "This verse addresses the infidels through the Holy Prophet ﷺ" — he is the one made to speak them.

## "For a little while" — *qalīlan*
