Everything in ayah 46 hinges on that one small word, and Ibn Kathir defines it without decoration: **"for a period of time that is short, small and brief."** Not *a little food* — a little *time*. The permission is real; the clock on it is the point.

Ibn Kathir then sets two other ayat beside this one as similar statements of Allah:

- **"We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to a great torment"** (31:24). The same word, *qalīlan*, and the same shape: brief enjoyment, then compulsion — they are *obliged*, with no say in it.
- **"Verily, those who invent a lie against Allah will never be successful. (A brief) enjoyment in this world! And then unto Us will be their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment because they used to disbelieve"** (10:69–70). Here the enjoyment is named for what it is — brief, and confined to this world — with the return and the torment following it.

Placed together by Ibn Kathir, these are not one isolated taunt but a recurring way the Qur'an describes the arrangement: a short span of enjoyment, and then what comes after it.

**"Verily, you are criminals"** is the reason clause, and Ibn Kathir reads it forward to what it entails: **"meaning, then you all will be driven to the fire of Hell which has already been mentioned."** The word carries a destination inside it.

## Ayah 48: they will not bow

**"And when it is said to them: 'Bow down yourself!' They bow not down."**

This is the diagnosis behind the sentence. The classical commentators read the word *rukūʿ* here in two ways, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports both.

**The first, which Maʿārif says is the view of most commentators:** *rukūʿ* is used here "in its primitive sense" — its root, everyday sense of *to bow down and submit*. On this reading the ayah is about the whole posture of a life: "when they were told to submit to the Divine commands, they refused to comply." The bowing demanded is not only of the back but of the will.

**The second, which Maʿārif attributes to "some scholars":** *rukūʿ* is taken in its technical sense — the bowing that is one of the postures of the prayer. Then the verse means, in Maʿārif's words, "when they are called to prayer, they refused to pray." Maʿārif explains the figure of speech involved: "The rukūʿ is a part of the prayer, but it refers here to the whole prayer" — a part named for the whole. (Maʿārif cites *Rūḥ* for this discussion.)

Ibn Kathir takes this second line and specifies it further, to the congregation: "when these ignorant disbelievers are ordered to pray with the congregation (of believers), they refuse and turn away from it arrogantly."

Whichever reading one takes, the refusal is the same refusal, seen either in the whole of a life or in the one act where submission becomes visible: a fixed time, someone else's call, other people beside you, and your face brought low. Note Ibn Kathir's word for how they turn away — **arrogantly**. It is not that they *could not* bow; it is that they would not stoop.

There is a quiet, uncomfortable mirror here for those who do believe. If refusing to bow is the mark of the denier, then the health of a believer is measured in the same place: in whether, when it is said *bow*, he bows — when the call comes at an inconvenient hour, when the command of Allah cuts across what he wanted, when obedience costs him standing among people.

## The refrain (47, 49)

**"Woe on that Day to the deniers!"** falls after each stroke. Ayah 46 states the charge; 47 pronounces the woe. Ayah 48 gives the evidence; 49 pronounces the woe again — and ayah 49 is its last sounding in the surah.

The rhythm matters. The verdict is not argued into existence at the end of a long case; it is repeated after each item, as though the case were already closed and each new fact merely confirmed it. And the ones addressed are always *al-mukadhdhibīn*, the deniers — those who called it a lie. The refrain does not say "woe to the sinners" but woe to those who denied that Day; in a surah about that Day, the ruinous thing is the denial itself.

## Ayah 50: the question with no answer

**"So what message (*ḥadīth*) after this would they believe in?"**

*Ḥadīth* here carries its plain sense of *speech, statement, discourse* — Ibn Kathir renders the ayah "Then in what statement after this will they believe?", Maʿārif as "Now, in which discourse, after this, will they believe?" The referent of *this* is the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir: **"if they do not believe in this Qur'an, then what talk will they believe in?"** — and he sets alongside it a parallel verse: **"Then in which speech after Allah and His Ayat will they believe?"** (45:6).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds why the question is unanswerable. The Qur'an "is the last Book of Allah which explains its message and wisdom most lucidly, excellently, eloquently, elegantly, and its arguments most convincingly. Its style is extremely effective and the admonition soul-capturing." Then the conclusion: **"If they do not believe in such a Book, then for which word are they waiting?"** Maʿārif also notes the register of the ayah — "This is to express disappointment in them."

That is the end of the surah's argument. Nothing further is coming; no clearer speech is being held in reserve. A person who turns from this has not run out of evidence. And the question is left open, unanswered, hanging — the last thing the surah says to them.

## What to do when you reach this ayah

Because ayah 50 is a question flung at those who will not believe, there is a beautiful response the believer makes on his own behalf. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that a Hadith narrative instructs that **when one recites this verse, he should say "I believe in Allah"** — you answer the question by stepping out of the group being questioned. (Maʿārif reports this as a Hadith narrative without naming a collection, so it is passed on here exactly as it is reported there, with no wording or attribution added.)

Maʿārif also gives the ruling on where this is said: "This statement must be made outside the prayer, or in voluntary prayer. He must abstain from this statement in obligatory and Sunnah prayer," noting that "Hadith narratives are clear on this point." Maʿārif closes the discussion with the scholar's habitual caution: "And Allah knows best!"

So the surah that has delivered warning after warning ends by handing the listener something small and concrete enough to act on immediately. The deniers eat and enjoy for a little while, and they will not bow. The one who has heard the surah properly does the opposite of both: he bows when he is told to bow, and when the last question comes — *what discourse after this will you believe?* — he answers it, *I believe in Allah.*

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary here with the words: "This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat Al-Mursalat, and all praise and thanks are due to Allah. He is the Giver of success and security."
